title: The Man Who Sang an Odyssey

lines.text: In 1935, a man who couldn't read began singing.
Days later, he stopped. The song was more than 12,000 lines long.
lines.say: Days later, he stopped. The song was more than twelve thousand lines long.

lines.text: His name was Avdo Međedović, of Bijelo Polje, in what is now Montenegro.
lines.say: His name was Ahv-doh Meh-jeh-doh-vitch, of Bee-yeh-lo Poh-lyeh, in what is now Montenegro.

lines.text: He had learned the tale by hearing a friend read it aloud, five or six times.
The printed version ran to about 2,160 lines. Avdo had, shall we say, expanded.
lines.say: The printed version ran to about two thousand one hundred and sixty lines. Ahv-doh had, shall we say, expanded.

lines.text: You would assume a prodigious memory. So did the singers themselves.
The man taking it down was Milman Parry, a young Harvard classicist, and his real quarry was Homer.
Homer's ships, Parry noted, are swift 'even when drawn up on land.'
The phrase fits the metre, not the moment.
Avdo wasn't reciting. He was building each line as he sang, from ready-made phrases and familiar scenes.
lines.say: Ahv-doh wasn't reciting. He was building each line as he sang, from ready-made phrases and familiar scenes.

lines.text: It has a name: oral-formulaic composition. The story holds steady. The words change.
Given a song of 2,294 lines he had never heard, he sang it back at 6,313.
lines.say: Given a song of two thousand two hundred and ninety-four lines he had never heard, he sang it back at six thousand three hundred and thirteen.

caption: He couldn't read, yet his song outgrew the book he learned it from by about ten thousand lines. Oral-formulaic composition explains how. A true story, fact-checked. Tomorrow: Economics. Curiouser No. 11
